context: An image pyramid stores an image at a sequence of resolutions. Each level is a smoothed copy of the one before, subsampled by a fixed ratio $q$, usually $2$ \cite{burt1981fast,burt1983laplacian}. The design literature constrains the generating kernel of one step. Burt and Adelson require it to be separable, normalized, symmetric and of equal contribution \cite[p.~533]{burt1983laplacian}, and Meer, Baugher and Rosenfeld require it to be good for one decimation \cite{meer1987frequency}. Burt observed that the equivalent kernels of the levels approach one shape \cite{burt1981fast}. What the literature does not state is a property of the whole family of kernels: every level looks like every other on its own grid. As an axiom, this is covariance under the dilations by $q^n$, $n \in \ZZ$, which leaves every other dilation optional.

\paragraph{Relation to the literature.} Each octave of the \Matern{} pyramid is one implicit heat step, and the step sizes grow geometrically. In Burt's hierarchy the kernel that takes the image to level $l$ is the generating kernel convolved with its dilates up to that level [\sscite{burt1981fast}, (2)--(4), pp.~21--23]. This last subsection returns to the classical pyramids. They smooth with a finite mask, applied separably [\sscite{burt1983laplacian}, p.~533]. The mask is a five-tap mask of Burt's family or a B-spline mask. The binomial $\tfrac1{16}[1,4,6,4,1]$ is in Burt's family [\sscite{burt1981fast}, p.~24]. No such mask is a step of any family that is continuous in scale, whatever its symmetry or covariance.

Clause (2) of the next proposition shows that the binomial mask has a refinable law, the cubic B-spline. Clause (1) reads Burt's observation that the rescaled equivalent weights approach one shape [\sscite{burt1981fast}, Obs.~1, p.~24]. The shape is approached and never reached, since no equivalent weight is the $q$-dilate of the one before.

The examples of Section~\ref{sec:pyramid-strata} separate the strata on the line too. At $d = 1$ the uniform law on the sphere of radius $h$ is $\tfrac12(\delta_h + \delta_{-h})$. The family of Proposition~\ref{prop:stratum-one-example} is then Lindeberg's discrete scale space [\sscite{lindeberg1990scalespace}], with $\varpi_t = t\,\delta_h$. It is in the first stratum and not in the second. The family of Proposition~\ref{prop:stratum-two-example} is the \emph{geometric-jump pyramid}, whose jumps have the lengths $hq^i$, $i \in \ZZ$. It is in the second stratum and not in the third. With these witnesses Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-strata-strict} separates the strata on the line. No kernel $\mu_{0,t}$, $t > 0$, of a $q^{\ZZ}$-covariant family is carried by a lattice $\xi\ZZ$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:no-lattice-kernel}).

The kernel at the knots that clause (2) gives has a classical meaning. It is the equivalent weighting function of Burt and Adelson [\sscite{burt1983laplacian}, p.~533], run downward in scale: $T_{q^{-1}}w * \dots * T_{q^{-M}}w$ is the equivalent weight of $M$ levels rescaled to the finest grid. Its limit is carried by no lattice, as Proposition~\ref{prop:no-lattice-kernel} requires. Between the knots the ladder leaves a choice. The families that carry it differ in how each atom of the mask is switched on across one octave, and Section~\ref{sec:line-phase-entropy} of the supplement compares them.

The pyramid also has a twin in time, through the \emph{subordination bridge} of \prog{V-cone v0.1}{\S 4}. The bridge substitutes $\sigma = r^2/2$. It reads a function of the frequency $r$ as a function of the Laplace variable $\sigma$ of a subordinator, an increasing \Levy{} process used as a random clock. Then $F_q(r) = \sum_{i \ge 1}\log(1 + 2c^2q^{-2i}\sigma)$. This is the exponent, in the Laplace variable $\sigma$, of Lindeberg's time-causal limit kernel with ratio $q^2$ and constant $2c^2$, a cascade of first-order integrators in time. Lindeberg defines that kernel by an infinite product of first-order factors [\sscite{lindeberg2016time}, Sect.~5, (38), p.~62] and realizes it by recursive first-order filters [\sscite{lindeberg2016time}, Sect.~6.2, p.~64]. The ratio and the constant are this paper's reading of his product.

Burt and Adelson's Laplacian pyramid [\sscite{burt1983laplacian}, p.~535] is a \emph{difference} of Gaussians, named after the Laplacian it approximates. On the Gaussian pyramid the level difference is $I - e^{\tau\Delta}$ applied to the finer level, with $\tau$ proportional to $(q^2 - 1)t^2$. Formally this is a series in all powers of $\Delta$. Its first term alone is a Laplacian, and it dominates only as $q \downarrow 1$. That comparison is heuristic and is not proved here.

A pyramid applies one small mask at every level, and the classical criteria judge that mask on its own \cite[p.~533]{burt1983laplacian}, \cite{meer1987frequency}. This paper judged it by another standard. Covariance under one ratio $q$ requires the mask to be the step between two levels of a family of kernels continuous in scale. The levels of the pyramid are then the image smoothed by kernels of that family. The questions are which masks have such a family, and how much of it the mask fixes.

The strata place the pyramids among the families of scale space. The dilations under which a symmetric family is covariant form $\{1\}$, some $q^{\ZZ}$, or all of $(0,\infty)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:family-dilations}(2)). So covariance under the powers of one ratio is the only case between none and every dilation. For isotropic families each stratum is strictly larger than the next (Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-strata-strict}). The pyramids of stratum~2 therefore form a wider class than the fully covariant families that the isotropic paper classifies \prog{iso v0.1}{Thm.~3.6, p.~13}. Lindeberg's scale space for discrete signals \cite{lindeberg1990scalespace} lies in stratum~1 and not in stratum~2 (Proposition~\ref{prop:lindeberg-stratum-one} of the supplement). It is no pyramid in this sense.

Stratum~2 holds many families, so a designer still needs a reason to choose one. On the line the count of local extrema gives that reason \prog{V-selection v0.1}{\S4}. In the plane a bound on the value at a local maximum takes its place. Among the isotropic families covariant under $q$, the \Matern{} pyramid is, up to the gauge, the one whose every octave stage has the implicit-Euler maximum principle (Theorem~\ref{thm:selection-stratum-two}(2)). Its octave step is one Helmholtz resolvent, the law $L_{ct}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:matern-pyramid}). The difference of the levels $t$ and $qt$ is $-c^2t^2$ times the Laplacian of the coarser one (Proposition~\ref{prop:laplacian-pyramid}). So for this family the level difference of the Laplacian pyramid of Burt and Adelson \cite{burt1983laplacian}, taken on the continuum before any decimation, is a Laplacian.

Sequences of implicit heat steps with geometrically growing step sizes occur in nonstationary iterated Tikhonov regularization \cite[pp.~38--39]{hanke1998nonstationary}. The decimation between them was not found in that literature. Nor was a covariant family through them, unique up to the gauge under the implicit-Euler principle. The selection cannot be read off the line either. The isotropic classes of one ratio shrink strictly with the dimension (Proposition~\ref{prop:what-does-not-lift-chain}), so the classification on the line does not carry to $\RR^d$ through marginals.

\emph{The families are positive, symmetric and continuous in scale.} Every kernel here is a probability law, so a mask with a negative weight is outside every statement. Burt's five-tap generating kernel with central weight $a > 1/2$, which has negative outer weights, is one \cite[p.~533]{burt1983laplacian}. Symmetry is required of every family studied, and rotation invariance where a result says isotropic. Proposition~\ref{prop:no-bounded-step} requires neither. Continuity in scale is the hypothesis that excludes the finite masks (Proposition~\ref{prop:no-bounded-step}). Each classical constraint on a mask is a condition at one level. Normalization is (A5) and symmetry is (A3). Burt's equal contribution, that every fine node contributes the same total weight to the coarse level [\sscite{burt1983laplacian}, p.~533], is the condition that the subsampled convolution preserve unit mass on the grid. Separability is the product structure of the frame families of \prog{affine v0.1}{Prop.~F.1, p.~93}. None of the four constrains the family across levels. Burt and Adelson observed that an equivalent weighting function resembles the Gaussian [\sscite{burt1983laplacian}, p.~533]. For the binomial mask Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-pyramids-approximate}(3) identifies the limit, and it is not Gaussian: the rescaled equivalent weights tend to the cubic B-spline, of excess kurtosis $-\tfrac3{10}$.

The generator of a Thorin exponent is a sum of Laplace-kernel differences \prog{V-cone v0.1}{Prop.~6.4(4), p.~58}, stated there for $a = 0$ and for $g \in C^2$ with $g$ and $g''$ bounded. Since each octave step is $L_{ct}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:matern-pyramid-line}(1)), the level differences $u(t) - u(qt) = (I - L_{ct})u(t)$ of its Laplacian pyramid [\sscite{burt1983laplacian}] are Laplace-kernel differences, the atomic generators of the Thorin class. The Laplacian pyramid of the Gaussian family is, in the same way, a bank of differences of Gaussians.

A time-causal family smooths a signal in time using only its past, and its kernels are laws on $[0,\infty)$ with Laplace exponents $H(s)$. The subordination bridge of Section~\ref{sec:matern-levels} of the paper turns such an exponent into the spatial exponent $H(\omega^2/2)$. It carries Lindeberg's time-causal limit kernel of ratio $q^2$ and constant $2c^2$ to the \Matern{} pyramid. Lindeberg defines that kernel as an infinite product of first-order factors [\sscite{lindeberg2016time}, Sect.~5, (38), p.~62], from which the ratio and the constant are read, and realizes it by recursive first-order filters [\sscite{lindeberg2016time}, Sect.~6.2, p.~64]. The limit $F_\infty$ of $\ell F_q$ in (\ref{eq:line-e8}) is the symmetric Thorin exponent with the log-uniform density $d\theta/\theta$ above the cutoff $1/c$, and it has no Gaussian part.

Lindeberg's discrete scale space is exact but not a pyramid (Proposition~\ref{prop:lindeberg-stratum-one}), since its grid is a preferred length. The grid refinement that makes it covariant, the geometric-jump pyramid of Proposition~\ref{prop:discrete-gaussian-pyramid}, lies in stratum (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-line} and not in stratum (3), and its kernels are no longer lattice laws. Lindeberg characterizes the discrete Gaussian as the unique discrete kernel with non-creation and a semigroup law [\sscite{lindeberg1990scalespace}]. Without the semigroup law, non-creation leaves a class of kernels in place of one family \prog{V-selection v0.1}{Remark~4.15}. No non-creation property is claimed here for the geometric-jump pyramid. The next proposition shows that neither of the line's two tools, lattice counting and \Polya{} frequency, applies to it.

Multiresolution analysis [\sscite{mallat1989theory}, (2)--(8), p.~676] is the nearest axiomatic neighbour. Its levels are nested dyadic subspaces and projections onto them, with no positivity, no non-creation and no hemigroup law. The scaling relation of its scaling function $g$, $g = \sum_kc_k\,g(2\,\cdot - k)$, is the knot relation of Definition~\ref{def:self-decomposable} without the requirement that the residual be infinitely divisible. The theory of this section is discrete in scale on continuous space. By the pyramid principle of Proposition~\ref{prop:no-lattice-kernel-line}(2), sampling a $q^{\ZZ}$-covariant family at scale $q^nt$ on the grid $q^nh\ZZ$ stores the same array at every level. The axioms do not fix $h/t$, the sampling density relative to the scale. That is the anti-aliasing trade-off which Meer and coauthors optimize for one decimation [\sscite{meer1987frequency}]. The sampled Laplace family is an exact cascade on the grid, its subsample is exact in sense (ii) of Definition~\ref{def:exact-senses}, and the grid pyramid of sampled \Matern{} levels is exact in sense (i) at its first level and at no later one (Proposition~\ref{prop:sampled-laplace-exact}). How much a level aliases is measured, for these pyramids, in further work.
